payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Draft: Why Transfer Night Matters

[1] Every spring, the second-floor meeting room at the Harlan Ferry Public Library fills with folding chairs, a dented coffee urn, and people who are not sure they belong there. [2] Community college is a good thing for a lot of people. [3] Our annual Transfer Night, held this year on Thursday, April 17, brings advisors from Calloway Valley Community College and two state universities to answer questions one at a time.

[4] Last year I met a man named Arturo Pell, who had left high school at seventeen to work in his uncle's tire shop. [5] At forty-one, he had just finished an associate degree at Calloway Valley, and he was trying to figure out which of his credits would count toward the nursing program at Ridgeline State University. [6] An advisor spent twenty minutes with him going over a printed transfer agreement, the sheet listed every Calloway Valley course that Ridgeline would accept. [7] He left with a plan and a highlighted copy of that sheet folded into his jacket pocket.

[8] Arturo's story is not unusual. [9] Many students start at community colleges because tuition is lower, because classes meet at night, or because they need time to rebuild confidence after a rough start somewhere else. [10] Transfer pathways are basically like a whole bunch of agreements and stuff that colleges make so that what you learn at one place gets counted at another place, which is really important. [11] Without them, a returning student can lose a semester or more retaking classes he or she has already passed.

[12] Anyway, that is pretty much what the night is about. [13] Hope to see you there.

el_passage.title: Draft: Why Transfer Night Matters
paragraphs: Every spring, the second-floor meeting room at the Harlan Ferry Public Library fills with folding chairs, a dented coffee urn, and people who are not sure they belong there.
Community college is a good thing for a lot of people.
Our annual Transfer Night, held this year on Thursday, April 17, brings advisors from Calloway Valley Community College and two state universities to answer questions one at a time.
Last year I met a man named Arturo Pell, who had left high school at seventeen to work in his uncle's tire shop.
At forty-one, he had just finished an associate degree at Calloway Valley, and he was trying to figure out which of his credits would count toward the nursing program at Ridgeline State University.
An advisor spent twenty minutes with him going over a printed transfer agreement, the sheet listed every Calloway Valley course that Ridgeline would accept.
He left with a plan and a highlighted copy of that sheet folded into his jacket pocket.
Arturo's story is not unusual.
Many students start at community colleges because tuition is lower, because classes meet at night, or because they need time to rebuild confidence after a rough start somewhere else.
Transfer pathways are basically like a whole bunch of agreements and stuff that colleges make so that what you learn at one place gets counted at another place, which is really important.
Without them, a returning student can lose a semester or more retaking classes he or she has already passed.
Anyway, that is pretty much what the night is about.
Hope to see you there.

provenance.note: Fictional draft; all names, places and institutions invented.

blueprint.purpose: To announce the library's annual Transfer Night and persuade adult readers, especially those returning to school, that community college transfer pathways offer a real second chance
blueprint.audience: Patrons of a small-town public library, including adults who left school early and parents of college-bound teenagers
blueprint.claim: Transfer pathways turn community college into a reliable route to a four-year degree, so readers considering a second start should come to Transfer Night
blueprint.theme: community college transfer pathways and the idea of a second chance

planned_flaws.flaw: Vague thesis that does not preview the post's argument or require proof
Comma splice joining two independent clauses
Wordy, vague, overly casual definition of transfer pathways
Abstract definition lacks a clarifying comparison for unfamiliar readers
Does not address readers who see community college as a lesser fallback
Flat, offhand conclusion that gives no invitation, details, or return to the second-chance idea

payload.theme: community college transfer pathways and the idea of a second chance

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 9 that addresses parents of college-bound teenagers who believe community college is a lesser choice than starting at a university. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Universities are often prestigious places, and many parents understandably dream of seeing their children attend one.
options.why: Reinforces the parents' belief rather than answering it, undercutting the writer's claim.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Honestly, anyone who still looks down on community college in this day and age just has not been paying attention.
options.why: Insults the very readers the writer hopes to persuade, likely alienating rather than reassuring them.
options.label: wrong_tone

options.text: Some returning adults also choose community college because it lets them keep a full-time job while they study.
options.why: Addresses adult learners, not the parents of teenagers named in the goal.
options.label: wrong_scope

issues.issue: Sentence 2 is intentionally vague (planned thesis flaw). It does not preview the argument about transfer pathways or the second-chance claim. This matches the blueprint and is a repairable weakness.
Sentence 6 is an intentional comma splice ('...transfer agreement, the sheet listed...'). It matches the blueprint and is repairable.
Sentence 10 is intentionally wordy and casual ('basically like a whole bunch of agreements and stuff') and lacks an analogy. It matches the blueprint for both concision and analogy repairs.

Sentence 9 gives reasons students start at community college but never addresses readers who view it as a lesser fallback. This is a planned flaw, and the sentence is a workable place to add an audience-aware revision.
Sentences 12-13 are an intentionally flat conclusion ('Anyway... Hope to see you there') with no time, place, or return to the second-chance theme, as the blueprint calls for.

The title header reads 'ALTON original passage', an apparent stray label that should be removed before delivery. Also, the flaw ids in the blueprint list sentence 10 twice and sentence 9 after it, but the passage is consistent with them.

The passage uses only fictional institutions (Harlan Ferry Public Library, Calloway Valley Community College, Ridgeline State University) and a fictional patron, with no real statistics or real-world claims. The anecdote and register read as a plausible human library blogger, and the passage does not resemble a known text.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
The Number Seven Bus

¶1 Lenore Quist drove the number seven bus for the Pell's Landing schools for twenty-two years and never once left a child at the curb because the clock said she could. She kept a shoebox of spare mittens under the driver's seat. She knew which kids needed a louder good morning and which needed none at all. When she died last Tuesday, at fifty-eight, of the kidney disease that had been chasing her for two years, the town did what towns do: it brought casseroles, lowered the flag at the depot, and opened the fundraising page one more time to see the final figure. Fifty-three thousand, four hundred dollars. I want to honor that figure, and I want to tell the truth about it, and I am not sure the two can be done in the same breath.

¶2 The page went up in March of last year, built by her niece at the kitchen table while Lenore protested from the next room that she did not want her face on the internet. The niece won. The photograph showed Lenore in her reflective vest, one hand on the folding door, grinning at someone out of frame. Within nine days the page passed its first goal; within a month it had covered the share of dialysis the insurance would not, the gas to a clinic forty miles away, and three months of rent she lost when she could no longer sit behind the wheel. People she had driven as six-year-olds, now with mortgages of their own, wrote notes beneath their donations. One simply said: you waited for me in the snow.

¶3 Here is the part the eulogies have skipped. Four streets over lived a man named Aurelio Dansk, a night-shift machinist with the same disease, the same clinic, and the same forty-mile drive. His page, which his daughter built with the same template, raised eleven hundred dollars. He was not less sick, and he was not less deserving, unless we have quietly decided that deserving means being known, being photographed well, and having driven half the county's children to school. He was simply a man whom fewer people had met, and the arithmetic of charity is pitiless about that.

¶4 I will concede what the defenders of these pages say, because it is true: the money was real, and so was the comfort. Lenore read every note aloud, and her niece told me that on the worst mornings the page was the first thing she opened, before the pill organizer, before the coffee. Nobody who gave did anything wrong; they did, in fact, something lovely. But a lifeboat is not a harbor, and we should stop describing the boat as though it were the shore. A system in which the sick must audition for their own survival is not generous; it has outsourced its stinginess to the kindness of neighbors and then taken credit for the kindness.

¶5 There is an old distinction worth reviving here, between charity and justice. Charity is what one person chooses to give; justice is what no person should have to ask for. When we blur the two, letting the warmth of the first stand in for the absence of the second, we make the Aurelios of the world invisible and the Lenores into proof that the arrangement works. It does not work. It worked for her, for a while, because she was a story that was easy to tell, and even that was not enough in the end.

¶6 So here is what I would ask you to remember, you who gave twenty dollars or two hundred. Remember the mittens, the snow, the grin at the folding door. Remember also that you were asked, out of your own pockets and on nine days' notice, to do something that should never have fallen to you at all. Lenore would have disliked this column; she hated being made an example of. But she waited for every child, including the ones nobody else was watching for, and I can think of no better instruction for the rest of us.

provenance.note: Entirely fictional tribute column; all names, places and figures invented.

blueprint.speaker: Teodor Brandvik, a longtime columnist for the fictional Harrow County Ledger who knew Lenore Quist personally
blueprint.audience: Residents of Pell's Landing and the surrounding county who read the paper and, in many cases, donated to Lenore's fundraising page
blueprint.exigence: The death of Lenore Quist, a beloved school bus driver, after a widely shared medical crowdfunding campaign raised 53,400 dollars; the town is celebrating the figure, and the columnist feels the celebration hides an uncomfortable truth
blueprint.purpose: To honor Lenore sincerely while arguing that the success of her campaign, set beside a neighbor's failed one, exposes a system that rations care by popularity, and to redirect the readers' generosity toward a demand for structural change
blueprint.context: An obituary-style tribute column in a small-town newspaper, written within a week of the death, addressed to a community that regards the fundraising total as a point of pride
blueprint.claim: Crowdfunding gave Lenore real money and real comfort, but a system in which the sick must audition for survival is not generous; it has outsourced its stinginess to neighbors, and the community's kindness should not be mistaken for justice
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: P1 establishes Lenore's character through concrete anecdote and sets up the tension between honoring the figure and telling the truth. P2 narrates the campaign's success and the warmth behind it. P3 shifts tone and introduces the contrasting case of Aurelio Dansk, whose nearly identical situation raised almost nothing, isolating popularity as the deciding variable. P4 concedes the real benefits of the page, then rebuts with the lifeboat/harbor metaphor and the central claim about outsourced stinginess. P5 supplies the charity/justice distinction that explains why confusing the two makes the Aurelios invisible. P6 returns to direct address, asking donors to remember both Lenore and the fact that the burden should never have fallen on them.

devices.function: Opens with concrete details of Lenore's care for children to establish her character and the writer's firsthand knowledge
The colon introduces the town's ritual responses, ending pointedly on checking the fundraising figure
A long sentence of accumulated town rituals followed by the bare fragment of the dollar figure gives the number weight and ambiguity
The two fundraising totals, 53,400 dollars versus 1,100 dollars, are the comparative core of the argument
Narrates the campaign's creation and success to show the warmth it generated before the writer complicates it
The colon sets off the donor's note so that its plain words land with maximum pathos
The note about waiting in the snow and the image of opening the page before the pill organizer make the comfort of the campaign emotionally real
Shifts from elegiac tribute to pointed critique, signaling that the column will not be a conventional eulogy

tone_shifts.to: intimate, direct exhortation to the readers

blueprint.counterargument: Defenders of crowdfunding pages say the money is real and the comfort is real, and that donors do something good; the writer concedes both fully, then argues that a lifeboat is not a harbor and that the system has merely outsourced its stinginess to neighbors.

payload.theme: the ethics of crowdfunding for medical bills

items.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.text: persuade readers who donated to Lenore's page that their money would have been better directed toward less visible patients such as Aurelio Dansk

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 4 and paragraph 5?

options.text: Paragraph 4 presents the view of crowdfunding's defenders, and paragraph 5 introduces new evidence about Aurelio Dansk that refutes that view

items.stem: The writer's phrasing "you who gave twenty dollars or two hundred" in paragraph 6 most likely serves to

"making the second clause noticeably longer to signal that justice is the more complicated and contested of the two concepts" is incorrect: The clauses are nearly equal in length and the passage never calls justice complicated; its point is that justice is simply what should not have to be requested.
"balancing the two clauses so evenly that the terms appear interchangeable, preparing the reader to accept the blurring the writer describes" is incorrect: The balance sharpens the difference rather than erasing it; the following sentence treats blurring the two as the error that makes 'the Aurelios of the world invisible.'
"subordinating the clause about justice to the clause about charity so that justice appears to follow as a consequence of giving" is incorrect: The clauses are coordinate, joined by a semicolon with neither dependent on the other; the passage argues charity cannot substitute for justice, not that one produces the other.

issues.issue: The phrase 'the arithmetic of charity is pitiless' and the 'lifeboat is not a harbor' contrast lean slightly on familiar rhetorical formulas, though they are deployed with specific local detail.
The 'ALTON original passage' header line is a labeling artifact that should be stripped before publication.
The planned flaw (admitting Lenore would have disliked the column) is present as intended and is recovered by the final sentence; it works as designed but is subtle for students to detect.
